clue.text: Limit kindness? No one turned away

indicators.note: a thing turned round faces the other way, so the letters it marks are read from their far end back
to send something away is to have it gone, so what it points at leaves the word entirely

parts.note: kindness shown to someone in trouble is compassion
'No' plus I for one spells NOI, and read the other way that is the ION which goes

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a grumble about rationed kindness, so 'No one' looks like a phrase rather than letters to be turned round and thrown out.
explanation.definitionFit: A compass is the range or scope a thing covers, as in 'beyond my compass', so 'Limit' points at extent rather than at the navigator's needle.

clue.text: Do well to study question, eliminating unknown component

indicators.note: to eliminate a competitor is to knock them out of the contest, and here a letter is knocked out of the word

parts.note: to con something is to study it closely, an old sense kept alive by crosswords
a question put to someone is a query
algebra's unknown quantity is Y, and Y is the letter taken out of QUERY

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is sound exam advice, so nothing in it reads as an instruction; even 'eliminating' passes for revision strategy.
explanation.definitionFit: To conquer is to prevail over whatever you took on, and 'do well' is the mild everyday way of saying you came out on top.

clue.text: The writer's upset Times editor in confusion

indicators.note: to upset a thing is to tip it over, and a word tipped over in a down entry is read from the bottom up

parts.note: the writer of a clue is I, so 'the writer's' is I'M, tipped over
the times sign in arithmetic is a cross, X
Ed is the standard short form for an editor

explanation.walkthrough: The italics make 'Times' look like the newspaper, which is why the arithmetic reading takes so long to arrive.
explanation.definitionFit: Papers left mixed are papers left in a muddle, so the definition uses the sense of disordered rather than of two things blended.

clue.text: Civic dignitary possibly now alarmed

indicators.note: 'possibly' says the printed order is only one of the orders these letters could take, so try another

parts.note: the ten letters of NOW ALARMED, put in a different order

explanation.walkthrough: 'possibly' looks like the hedge a setter adds to an approximate definition, and it is really the instruction — a maybe and an order in one word.
explanation.definitionFit: An alderwoman is an elected member of a borough council senior to the ordinary councillors, so 'civic dignitary' names her office in the town hall.

clue.text: Knight embracing Queen and maiden, making you feel uncomfortable

indicators.note: to embrace someone is to put your arms right round them, so the knight closes on either side of what follows

parts.note: a knight is addressed as Sir
Qu. is the recognised short form of Queen
M is the cricket scorer's mark for a maiden over

explanation.walkthrough: Chess owns both a knight and a queen, so the surface holds together as a board position right up to the maiden — which belongs to cricket instead.
explanation.definitionFit: To squirm is to wriggle in discomfort, so the definition names the feeling that produces the movement rather than the movement itself.

clue.text: Little doctor's pronouncement, taking temperature

indicators.note: taking a thing is lifting it out of where it sat, so what follows is removed rather than added

parts.note: a medical officer is an MO, and the apostrophe-s carries on into the next word
a formal pronouncement is a dictum
temperature is T, and that is the letter lifted out of DICTUM

explanation.walkthrough: 'Little doctor' reads as one phrase and is really the seam of the clue: the definition stops after a single word.
explanation.definitionFit: A modicum is a small amount of something, so 'Little' is the noun use — 'he has little' — rather than the adjective the surface offers.

clue.text: Landed area in muddy surroundings for the army

indicators.note: surroundings are what lie all around a thing, so the muddy word closes around the rest

parts.note: ground thick with mud is miry
a bird that has landed has lit on its perch
A is the standard abbreviation for area

explanation.walkthrough: 'Landed area' reads as a plot of ground, which is exactly the wrong reading: the two words are separate pieces from quite different senses.
explanation.definitionFit: Something military belongs to the armed forces, so 'for the army' gives the adjective's job — of or for soldiers — rather than a noun.

clue.text: Avoid coarse cotton, dear
Face elevated argument over last of steampunk machinery

indicators.note: a piece raised up a down entry arrives bottom first, so the word it marks is read the other way
the last of a word is the single letter it finishes on, and nothing before it

parts.note: a clock has a face, and 'clock' is also slang for the human one
an argument is a row, raised up the entry so it reads WOR

indicators.note: in a down entry what is over something sits above it, so the face goes on top of the rest

parts.note: steampunK finishes on K

explanation.walkthrough: Unusually the surface and the answer agree — steampunk really is brass gears — so the misdirection has to live in the small word 'over'.
explanation.definitionFit: Clockwork is the wound spring-and-gear mechanism that drives a wind-up device, so 'machinery' names it by the class of thing it belongs to.

clue.text: One starts to seem crazy, drilling section of yacht with the wrong part

definitions.note: The answer is a participle and the definition a phrase, but 'was miscast' and 'was with the wrong part' say the same thing about an actor.

indicators.note: what a word starts to be is its opening letter, taken here from each word in turn

parts.note: the mast is the section of a yacht that carries the sail

indicators.note: a drill bores straight into the middle of a thing, which is where these letters end up

parts.note: I is one in Roman numerals
the openings of Seem and Crazy

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a boatyard job — drilling a yacht section, fitting the wrong part — and every word of it is really about the theatre.
explanation.definitionFit: An actor who is miscast has been handed a role they are wrong for, so the definition describes the casting rather than the actor.

clue.text: Cancel nine to begin with? Nine

indicators.note: what a word begins with is its opening letter, and that is as far as you read

parts.note: the letter nine begins with
nine in Roman numerals is IX

explanation.walkthrough: The same word twice, read two ways — English initial, then Roman numeral — which is why the second 'Nine' looks like a definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To nix a plan is to veto or scrap it, an Americanism from the German for nothing, so 'Cancel' is the plain verb sense.

clue.text: Cheat, repeating final letter of last answer?

parts.note: to repeat a thing is to double it

indicators.note: the final letter is the one a word stops on, and here it is the only part you take

parts.note: the entry numbered before this one is 9 across; it stops on X, and X is a cross

explanation.walkthrough: This one points out of itself at the grid, so it cannot be started until the entry numbered before it has already gone in.
explanation.definitionFit: To double-cross an accomplice is to betray them while pretending to be in league, so 'Cheat' names the treachery in one word.

clue.text: What insurer may do, governed by legal document (European)

parts.note: a country governed by a ruler is under them
a writ is the court's written order
E is the usual abbreviation for European

explanation.walkthrough: There is no indicator at all here — the pieces simply sit in order — so the only thing to spot is where the definition stops.
explanation.definitionFit: To underwrite a risk is to accept liability for it in return for a premium, which is precisely the business an insurer is in.

clue.text: Seabird a European country's repulsed

indicators.note: an attack that is repulsed is driven back the way it came, and so are these letters

parts.note: the indefinite article taken as itself
the UK is a European country, and the apostrophe-s adds an S

explanation.walkthrough: Read forwards the wordplay gives a different seabird entirely, which is the joke: the auks are in plain sight and facing the wrong way.
explanation.definitionFit: A skua is a big piratical gull of northern waters that chases other birds for their catch, so 'Seabird' places it by habitat.

clue.text: Describing pressure arising from wandering of erratic mob

indicators.note: something that wanders keeps to no fixed course, and letters that wander end up somewhere other than where they started

parts.note: the ten letters of ERRATIC MOB in a new order

explanation.walkthrough: 'Erratic' describes a mob perfectly and reads like a shuffling signal too — but it is the material, and 'wandering' is the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Barometric readings are of atmospheric pressure, the adjective taking its name from the barometer that measures it, so the sense is technical.

clue.text: Staff concealing a title for man, a strict disciplinarian

indicators.note: to conceal a thing is to keep it out of sight inside something else, which is where these letters go

parts.note: a staff carried as a stick is a rod
the article taken as itself
Mr is the everyday title for a man

explanation.walkthrough: The split falls after the first letter of the staff word, and a container that opens one letter in is very nearly invisible.
explanation.definitionFit: A ramrod was the rod that tamped a musket charge home, and the word came to name anyone rigidly upright and unbending about the rules.

clue.text: American mother keeping various curios in playing area

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold on to it, and a word that keeps another has it inside
when a thing may be various it takes more than one form, and so do these letters

parts.note: an American calls his mother Mom
the six letters of CURIOS in a different order

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a house full of knick-knacks, and 'various curios' is exactly the phrase you would use about them, so it never reads as an order.
explanation.definitionFit: A music room is the room set aside for playing instruments, so 'playing area' is fair on the musical sense of play rather than the sporting one.

clue.text: Arrangement of Take Four? How Brubeck might respond

definitions.note: The answer is a verb phrase while the definition asks how someone would react, so the swap needs 'he would' in front of it.

indicators.note: an arrangement is a piece of music written out afresh from the same material, which is what happens to these letters

parts.note: the eight letters of TAKE FOUR, rearranged

explanation.walkthrough: Brubeck's quartet recorded 'Take Five', and the italics dress the two words up as a real title — being one digit out is the whole joke.
explanation.definitionFit: To freak out is to lose your composure, which is what handing the man who recorded 'Take Five' a piece called 'Take Four' would provoke.

clue.text: Storms penetrating sheltered zone? Here's the small print on policy

indicators.note: to penetrate a thing is to get right inside it, so the storms end up within the sheltered word

parts.note: the lee is the side out of the wind
gales are storms of wind

explanation.walkthrough: Shelter and gales are opposites, so the surface reads as weather and the container hides inside the contradiction.
explanation.definitionFit: Legalese is the dense jargon lawyers draft contracts in, which is exactly what the small print of an insurance policy is made of.

clue.text: More than one report gets old after confusion

indicators.note: 'after' sets what comes before it behind what comes later, so the two pieces swap over on their way into the grid

parts.note: a mess is confusion
whatever gets old ages

explanation.walkthrough: The definition spells the plural out in words instead of adding an S, which is the setter being scrupulous — 'report' alone would not be fair.
explanation.definitionFit: A message is a communication sent from one person to another, so 'report' is the sense of an item of news passed on, counted here in the plural.

clue.text: Particle's energy absorbed by quiet child

indicators.note: a thing absorbed is taken up inside whatever absorbs it, so the letter goes within rather than beside

parts.note: to keep mum is to stay quiet
E is the physicist's symbol for energy
a son is a child

explanation.walkthrough: 'quiet child' reads as one description of a well-behaved infant, and the clue needs it as two unrelated words with a gap between them.
explanation.definitionFit: The mu meson is the older name for the muon, one of the fundamental particles, so 'Particle' names it by its place in physics.

clue.text: Under compulsion, Home Office initially agreed

indicators.note: an initial is the letter a name starts with, so only the openings of the two words are taken

parts.note: the openings of Home and Office, which is also the department's real abbreviation
to have agreed to something is to have OK'd it

explanation.walkthrough: The letters produce the very abbreviation the words already have, so the wordplay and the surface arrive in the same place and nothing jars.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone hooked on a drug or a habit cannot stop, so 'under compulsion' is the addiction sense rather than the angler's or the boxer's.

clue.text: Famous lover's lust for one with husband — apartment overturned

indicators.note: 'for one' offers the word before it as a single example, so lust is being given as an instance of something broader
turning a thing over puts what was at the bottom on top, so the assembled letters are read the other way

parts.note: lust is one of the seven deadly sins
H is the standard abbreviation for husband
somebody's pad is their apartment

explanation.walkthrough: Greek pastoral romance is a long way from a lustful husband in a flat, and that distance is the whole of the misdirection.
explanation.definitionFit: Daphnis is the shepherd hero of the Greek romance 'Daphnis and Chloe', so the definition names him by the story he is half of.

clue.text: Pen, mostly attractive — digital pen?

indicators.note: most of a word is all of it bar the final letter, so one letter is left behind

parts.note: a pig's pen is a sty
something attractive can be called lush

explanation.walkthrough: The clue prints 'pen' twice in unrelated senses — an enclosure for animals, then something you write with — and the dash is all that separates them.
explanation.definitionFit: A stylus is the pen-shaped tool you write on a touchscreen with, and 'digital' does double duty: of computers, and of the fingers.

clue.text: Spicy stuff: hint of masochism excellent

indicators.note: a hint is the barest trace of a thing, and the barest trace of a word is the letter it opens on

parts.note: the opening letter of masochism
something excellent is ace

explanation.walkthrough: Spice and a hint of masochism make one unpleasant picture, and that picture is all that holds the two halves of the clue together.
explanation.definitionFit: Mace is the spice made from the lacy red covering of the nutmeg, so 'spicy stuff' puts it in the kitchen rack, not the sergeant's hand.

clue.text: Tablet's revamped trendy element of pen-and-paper game

indicators.note: to revamp a thing is to make it over into a new shape out of the same old parts

parts.note: the seven letters of TABLETS made over
something trendy is hip

explanation.walkthrough: 'Tablet' and 'trendy' both belong to the gadget surface, which is why neither reads as raw material for a game played on squared paper.
explanation.definitionFit: In the grid game played on squared paper the battleship is the largest vessel you hide, so the definition names a piece rather than the game.

clue.text: Lots of people taking road through garden

indicators.note: a road running through a garden passes inside it, and that is where these letters sit

parts.note: to garden is to hoe
Rd is the abbreviation on any street sign

explanation.walkthrough: 'Garden' is a verb here and not a place, and in a clue of seven words that single reassignment is the whole difficulty.
explanation.definitionFit: A horde is a great swarming crowd on the move, from the Tartar word for a nomad camp, so 'lots of people' is the plain modern sense.

clue.text: Song — again my heart will soar? Not entirely

indicators.note: something that soars climbs, and a word climbing a down entry is read from the bottom upwards
you are not to take the whole phrase, only a run of letters sitting inside it

parts.note: agai(n my h)eart holds N MY H, and climbing the entry those letters read the other way

explanation.walkthrough: The romantic surface does all the work: nothing in 'again my heart' looks like material, and 'Not entirely' reads as a rueful afterthought.
explanation.definitionFit: A hymn is a song of praise sung in church, so 'Song' defines it by the wider class it belongs to rather than by what it is for.

clue.text: Fabulist, believer in markets, perhaps, keeping right-winger tense

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it inside, so the market word closes around what follows it

parts.note: 'perhaps' offers an example: one sort of believer in markets is a seller
a Tory sits on the right wing of British politics
T is the grammarian's abbreviation for tense

explanation.walkthrough: The politics are a decoy — a market believer and a right-winger belong in one sentence, and neither has anything to do with fables.
explanation.definitionFit: A fabulist tells fables and, by extension, tall tales, which is what a storyteller does; the definition is simply the more literary word.

clue.text: One avoiding loss in delivery round?

indicators.note: to avoid a place is to keep out of it, so the letter named stays outside the word

parts.note: a loss that finishes you is your ruin
one is the Roman numeral I, and it is the letter keeping clear

explanation.walkthrough: Cricket owns every word of the surface — a delivery, a round, avoiding a loss — and not one of them is doing that job in the parse.
explanation.definitionFit: A run is a fixed route covered regularly, as in a milk run or a paper run, so 'delivery round' is the transport sense.

clue.text: Candidate: a lot of negative votes about my selection?

indicators.note: a lot of a thing is nearly all of it, so the word arrives one letter short
to put something about a thing is to wrap it round, so the letters close on either side

parts.note: the noes are the votes cast against
whatever I pick out is mine

explanation.walkthrough: 'my selection' is the sly one: not a choice and not a coal seam, but the possessive — the thing that is mine.
explanation.definitionFit: A nominee is the person formally put forward for a post or an award, so 'Candidate' is the plain synonym for someone in the running.

clue.text: Religious groups gathering about things to be revealed?

indicators.note: to gather something in is to draw it inside, so the groups close around what follows

parts.note: sects are religious groups
RE is the business letter's 'about', as in 'Re: your enquiry'

explanation.walkthrough: A gathering of sects is a perfectly good picture in its own right, which is why 'gathering' never announces itself as an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: A secret is something withheld that could still come out, so the definition names them by what is waiting to happen to them.
